Adapted from Peters, Alves, and Onwudili (2023) Despite being one of the earliest certified pathways to SAF, the SIP process has seen less commercial activity and interest relative to other SAF pathways (e.g., HEFA, FT, ATJ). Unlike some other processes that can valorize low-cost waste streams (e.g., used cooking oil, industrial flue gases), SIP favors dedicated on-purpose production of sugar-rich crops, which can both increase the operating costs and intensify concerns with the “food versus fuel” land-use debate. Further, from a technical performance perspective, the current limits with respective fermentation yields combined with complex downstream purification contribute to a final SAF selling price that can be double or more of other SAF pathways (Grim et al. 2022). To date, SIP remains a niche pathway with minimal commercial interest beyond a small number of initial demonstration flights. 2.1.1.4 Alcohol-to-Jet The certified ATJ pathway is a TRL 8–9 technology that involves the upgrading and conversion of two alcohols, butanol and ethanol. Annex A5 (ATJ-SPK) of ASTM D7566 was approved in 2016 for SPK from iso-butanol (30% blend with petroleum) based on technology developed by Gevo. Later, the annex was expanded in 2018 to include SPK from ethanol based on technology developed by LanzaTech and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and raised the fuel blending limit up to 50% with petroleum (Holladay et al. 2020). Shown in Figure 13, the ATJ pathway comprises four key conversion steps: (1) alcohol dehydration to olefins (e.g., ethylene); (2) olefin oligomerization, where low-molecular-weight olefins are combined into a distribution of longer-chain olefins; (3) hydrogenation of olefins to saturate double bonds and increase energy content; and (4) separation and fractionation to the appropriate carbon range for target fuel applications consisting of primarily of paraffin and isoparaffin hydrocarbons. Although shown below in ‘maximum jet configuration’ producing ~90% SAF and 10% renewable diesel, similar to other pathways, the final product composition can be tuned based on the operating conditions during oligomerization. With this flexibility, operators can respond to market signals and change the product to as low as 25% SAF / 75% renewable diesel if desired (LanzaJet 2025). 16 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
